# Results — Study 665 (Titanic Syndrome)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
Bill Ohama's 1965 **Titanic Syndrome**: if the market prints a fresh 52-week high within
the last **7 trading sessions** and, on that reading, more stocks are hitting fresh
52-week **lows** than fresh highs, internal breadth has failed to confirm the new high
and a decline should follow. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last
complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprints
`d5002741f424` (Dow-30 panel) / `be8c9799b5f0` (^GSPC) / `322761c2a52f` (SPY).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes for the **30 current Dow Jones Industrial Average members** (4,548 rows), ^GSPC price-index close (4,548 rows) and SPY adjusted close (4,548 rows), 2008-06-02 → 2026-06-30 |
| Breadth basket | **hardcoded** list of the 30 current (2026) Dow members — a coarse, **survivorship-biased** proxy for the thousands of NYSE issues the 1965 rule was built on (see `docs/references.md`) |
| Signal | index (^GSPC) printed a fresh trailing-252-session high on any of the trailing 7 sessions (Ohama's window) **AND** that day's Dow-30 new-52-week-low count exceeds the new-52-week-high count |
| Clustering | consecutive signal sessions within **21 calendar days** merged into one cluster (Hindenburg-style convention on this desk, avoids double-counting one listing episode) |
| Events | **21** raw signal sessions → **13** clusters, 2011-02-24 → 2026-05-15 |
| Statistics | Welch *t* (signal vs a drift-matched random-entry baseline of the same count, and vs the plain unconditional monthly-sampled mean); one-sample Newey-West (HAC) *t*; Welch *t* on the false-alarm proportions; an empirical percentile test for the timer vs a random-timer control (1,000 draws) |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention: forward returns and the timer both enter/act at the **next session's close** after the signal is read (zero look-ahead); the timer pays **5 bps one-way** on every position transition |
| Data quirks (named) | "52-week high" (252-session trailing) stands in for Ohama's literal "new high in equities" — a true all-time high isn't computable from a panel that starts 2008-06 without pretending to data we don't have; this is the same free-data-computable proxy used across the desk's breadth studies |

**Survivorship, named on the Signal axis:** the Dow-30 basket is *current* membership.
Names removed from the index over the sample window (GE, Pfizer, Intel, Walgreens,
ExxonMobil, Raytheon, DowDuPont, …) are excluded, which plausibly **understates** the
true new-lows count during any of their idiosyncratic declines — the bias points
**against** the signal firing, the same direction named on the sibling
[167-hindenburg-omen](../167-hindenburg-omen/) study's S&P panel.

## The headline — forward SPY return: signal vs random-entry vs unconditional

| horizon | signal mean (n) | one-sample HAC *t* | random-entry mean (n) | unconditional mean (n) | Welch *t* (signal − random) | Welch *t* (signal − unconditional) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1d | **−9.0 bps** (13) | −0.45 | +0.9 bps (30) | +9.6 bps (216) | −0.39 | −0.76 |
| 5d | **+38.4 bps** (13) | +1.05 | −29.6 bps (29) | +31.1 bps (216) | +1.24 | +0.15 |
| 20d | **+23.1 bps** (13) | +0.16 | +46.2 bps (29) | +106.1 bps (215) | −0.12 | −0.43 |
| 60d | **+190.5 bps** (12) | +1.73 | +199.7 bps (29) | +300.1 bps (213) | −0.06 | −0.84 |

Every |Welch *t*| stays **well under 2** at every horizon, both against the
drift-matched random-entry control and the plain unconditional baseline. The sign even
flips across horizons (SPY is *down* on average the very next session after a signal,
then *up* — a coin flip's worth of noise, not a warning system). With only **13**
independent clusters in 18 years, the arithmetic is honest about its own limits, but
there is no hint of a systematic post-signal decline to certify even directionally.

## False-alarm rate — cluster followed by a ≥5% SPY drawdown within 60 sessions?

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| signal decline rate | **58.3%** (12 clusters) |
| base rate (random dates) | 54.9% (213 dates) |
| Welch *t* | **+0.22** |
| **false-alarm rate** | **41.7%** |

At first glance 58% sounds like a working warning light — until you notice that *any*
random day over this 2009-2026 tape (three corrections, a bear market, a pandemic crash)
already has a **54.9%** chance of a ≥5% drawdown somewhere in the next 60 sessions. The
gap (+3.4 points) is statistically indistinguishable from zero (*t* = 0.22). Roughly
**2 signals in 5** fire and nothing resembling a decline follows within the test window
— a textbook false-alarm machine, the same critique leveled at its cousin the
Hindenburg Omen ([167-hindenburg-omen](../167-hindenburg-omen/)).

## The timer — hold SPY, sit in cash for 20 sessions after each cluster

Enter cash the session *after* a cluster fires (zero look-ahead), 5 bps one-way cost per
transition.

| | buy & hold | Titanic timer |
|---|--:|--:|
| CAGR | +11.82% | **+12.21%** |
| annualized vol | 19.81% | 18.74% |
| Sharpe (cash = 0%) | 0.66 | **0.71** |
| max drawdown | −50.7% | −50.7% |
| sessions out of the market | — | 260 (26 transitions) |

The timer *nominally* beats buy-and-hold — but the max drawdown is **identical to the
decimal**, because the single worst drawdown on the tape (the 2008-09 financial crisis)
predates the earliest possible signal (a full 252-session lookback isn't available until
mid-2009) — the timer never had a chance to dodge it. The modest CAGR/Sharpe edge has to
be judged against a fair control, not buy-and-hold alone:

**Random-timer control** — same cluster count (13), same fixed 20-session exit window,
dates drawn uniformly at random, 1,000 draws:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| random-timer CAGR | mean **+10.93%**, sd 0.93% |
| real timer's percentile | **92nd** |
| one-sided *p* (random ≥ real) | **0.080** |

The real timer beats the *average* random placement (10.93% vs 12.21%) — but a
one-sided *p* of 0.08 misses the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar and isn't a certified edge. The more
plausible mechanism isn't "breadth divergence predicts a crash": entries *near a
52-week high* (the ATH-window condition alone, regardless of breadth) tend to sit right
before a **below-unconditional** average forward stretch (see the 20d/60d unconditional
column above vs the signal column) — sitting out then costs less forgone upside than
sitting out at a uniformly random time. That is a mild high-water-mark mean-reversion
artifact, not the Titanic Syndrome's stated crash-detection mechanism.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic Dow-30-sized panel (30 one-factor-correlated price paths, ρ ≈ 0.40 —
i.i.d. paths would make "half the panel diverges" spuriously common and would not be a
faithful null) with scheduled pseudo-Titanic days and a TUNABLE planted post-signal
crash; no network.

| world | clusters | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (crash = 0), **20 seeds** | 2–16 per seed | mean **−0.32** (sd 1.36), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 2/20 seeds** |
| planted crash = 15 bps/day × 30d (seed 665) | 5 | **−4.37** |

The detector stays quiet on all but 2 of 20 null seeds (close to the ≈1-in-20 rate you'd
expect from repeated small-sample testing, not a bias toward manufacturing
significance) and lights up sharply on a planted decline. *(A faithful-engine / power
check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Forward SPY returns after a Titanic-Syndrome cluster are
  statistically indistinguishable from both a drift-matched random-entry baseline and
  the plain unconditional mean at every horizon (1/5/20/60 sessions), max |Welch
  *t*| = 1.24. The false-alarm rate (41.7%) reflects a signal decline-rate (58.3%) that
  is itself indistinguishable from the tape's base rate (54.9%, *t* = 0.22). Only 13
  independent clusters in 18 years — the small-sample caveat is real, but there is no
  directional hint to chase, let alone certify. Survivorship (current Dow-30 membership)
  is named and, if anything, biases against the signal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Nothing to bank: the timer's modest paper edge over
  buy-and-hold (Sharpe 0.71 vs 0.66) sits at only the 92nd percentile of a random-timing
  control (one-sided *p* = 0.08, short of the *t* ≥ 2 bar), and the worst drawdown on the
  tape is identical whether or not you use the rule — the one crash it would have most
  wanted to dodge predates the earliest possible signal.
- **"False-alarm machine?" — CONFIRMED.** 41.7% of clusters fire and nothing resembling
  a decline follows within the test window; the "successful" 58.3% is not distinguishable
  from the market's own baseline hit rate. The same critique leveled at the Hindenburg
  Omen applies here, with the same arithmetic behind it.
